subtype: Approach: push through and hide it [Pitfall]
passage:
Come, sit. I'll tell you about my second year, Ganga. I'm Chaitanya, and back then I thought that if I admitted I was struggling, everyone would look at me differently. So I smiled at breakfast, cracked jokes in the lab, and said 'all fine!' to every message. Then I stopped replying to messages at all.

I skipped lunch most days and told the mess cook I'd eaten. By the fourth week my hands shook in practicals and I couldn't follow a single lecture. Rekha, who shared my bench, knocked on my door one evening and said, 'You're not okay, are you?' I nearly said 'I'm fine' again. It took me another two weeks after that to ask for help, and I lost a whole semester's momentum.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya tell the mess cook?
qa.a: That Chaitanya had eaten, even though lunch was skipped most days.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya afraid of when hiding the struggle?
qa.a: Chaitanya feared that admitting difficulty would make people look at Chaitanya differently, as weak.

qa.q: When Rekha knocked, what different choice could Chaitanya have made, and why?
qa.a: Chaitanya could have let Rekha in and said things were hard, because the knock was an opening, and every week of delay cost more energy.

qa.q: How did Rekha see Chaitanya's cheerful face before that evening?
qa.a: Rekha noticed something was wrong beneath the jokes, as the missed lunches and silence did not fit the smile.

grounding: An elder recalls hiding a struggle behind cheer, skipping meals and ignoring friends, which drained energy and delayed help.
